activities.topic: Introduction to Electricity in Daily Life

instructions: Walk around your house and observe carefully.
Find at least 10 things that use electricity.
Write their names in your notebook.

extra_challenge.task: Look outside your house or on the street and try to find 3 more things that use electricity.

think_and_answer: Which device in your home do you think uses the most electricity?
Which device uses the least electricity?
What happens in your house when electricity goes off?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss these answers with your parents or family members.
bonus_activity: Where is the electricity meter in your house?
How much electricity bill usually comes every month?

instructions: Go around your house and observe different electrical switches.
Find at least 5 switches that control electrical devices.
Write the device name next to each switch.

observation_task: Turn one switch ON and observe what happens.
Turn the same switch OFF and observe again.
think_and_answer: Why do you think a switch is needed in a circuit?
What would happen if there were no switches in our homes?
Why does the light turn OFF immediately when the switch is turned OFF?
bonus_activity: Find one device that works on battery instead of a switch
Examples: Remote control, Wall clock, Torch

instructions: Take 5–6 objects like pencils, spoons, pens, erasers.
Place them in a straight line on a table to create a path.
Roll a small ball or marble along the path.
Remove one object from the middle and try again.

extra_challenge.task: Create a longer path using more objects and test again.

think_and_answer: What happens when the path is complete?
What happens when one object is removed?
Why does electricity also need a complete path to travel?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss answers with parents or family members.
learning_outcomes: Understand the concept of a complete path
Relate real-life paths to electrical circuits
bonus_activity: Find one device at home that has wires connected to it
Follow the wire and observe where it starts and ends

activity_1.title: Slow Down the Flow
steps: Take a plastic bottle or glass of water.
Pour the water normally into another cup.
Place your finger slightly over the mouth of the bottle.
Pour the water again and observe how the water comes out slower.

activity_2.title: Store and Release
steps: Take a sponge, cloth, or small towel.
Dip it in water so it absorbs water.
Lift it and slowly squeeze it.
Observe how the water comes out slowly instead of all at once.

extra_exploration.task: Take a balloon and blow air into it. Hold the opening closed, then release the air slowly and observe how the air comes out gradually.

think_and_notice: Which object made the water flow slower?
Which object stored something and released it slowly?
Where do you see similar things happening in your home?
activities.discussion_instruction: Talk about this with your parents.

learning_outcomes.title: Observe flow control
learning_outcomes.description: Students understand that flow can be slowed or controlled.

learning_outcomes.title: Observe storage and release
learning_outcomes.description: Students experience how objects can store something and release it gradually.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect home observations to technology
learning_outcomes.description: Students begin relating daily-life phenomena to how machines and devices work.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop curiosity and experimentation skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students explore concepts through hands-on activities.

instructions: Collect 10 small objects from your house.
Group them based on similarities such as color, size, or shape.

extra_challenge.task: Look at the objects again and try to find patterns on them and guess what those patterns might mean.
examples: Lines or stripes on bottle caps

think_and_answer: How did you decide which objects belong in the same group?
Did any colors, numbers, or markings help you identify them?
Why do you think engineers use colors or markings on small components?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your ideas with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Recognize patterns and markings
learning_outcomes.description: Students identify visual patterns like colors, numbers, and symbols.

learning_outcomes.title: Classify objects based on features
learning_outcomes.description: Students group items using similarities such as color, size, or shape.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and analytical skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students carefully examine small details in objects.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand how markings convey information
learning_outcomes.description: Students begin to realize that colors or symbols can represent useful information in technology.

bonus_activity: Look around your house and find 3 objects that use color codes or symbols.
Examples: charging cables, batteries, switches, remote control buttons
Think about what those colors or symbols might indicate.

activity_1.title: Control with a Switch
steps: Find a light switch in your house.
Turn the switch ON and observe what happens.
Turn the switch OFF and observe again.
Repeat this 3–4 times and notice how the device responds.

activity_2.title: Press and Release
steps: Find a doorbell or a toy with a button.
Press the button and listen carefully.
Release the button.
Observe when the sound starts and when it stops.

extra_exploration.task: Find three buttons or switches in your home and press them to observe what happens.

think_and_notice: What happens when the switch is turned ON?
What happens when the switch is turned OFF?
What happens when you press and release a button?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand control of devices
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how switches control the working of electrical devices.

learning_outcomes.title: Recognize temporary and continuous actions
learning_outcomes.description: Students notice that some buttons work only while pressed, while others stay ON.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect daily experiences with technology
learning_outcomes.description: Students relate household switches and buttons to how machines are controlled.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and experimentation skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students learn through simple real-world exploration.

bonus_activity: Look around your house and find 5 different switches or buttons.
Examples: light switch, doorbell button, microwave button, TV remote, keyboard keys
Notice how each one controls something different.

activities.topic: Single Path and Multiple Path Concept
activities.activity_title: One Path vs Many Paths Challenge

activity_1.title: Single Path Experiment
steps: Place 4–5 books or boxes in a straight line on the floor.
Create a narrow walking path between them.
Ask one family member to walk through that path.
Observe how people have to move one after another in the same path.

activity_2.title: Multiple Paths Experiment
steps: Arrange the books in a way that two walking paths are created.
Ask two family members to walk through the paths at the same time.
Observe how movement becomes faster and easier when there are multiple paths.

extra_exploration.task: Look around your home and find two places where multiple paths exist and observe how movement happens through different routes.
examples: Two taps connected to one water tank

think_and_notice: What happens when everyone has to move through one single path?
What happens when there are multiple paths available?
Which situation allows things to move more easily?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand the concept of shared and separate paths
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how movement changes depending on the number of available paths.

learning_outcomes.title: Relate real-life paths to electrical systems
learning_outcomes.description: Students connect daily situations with how electricity can travel through different routes.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and reasoning skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how different arrangements affect movement.

learning_outcomes.title: Strengthen curiosity about how systems work
learning_outcomes.description: Students begin exploring how engineers design systems for better performance.

bonus_activity: Look at the lights in your home.
Turn ON two or three lights in different rooms.
Now switch one OFF.
Observe whether the other lights still stay ON.
Think about why that happens.

activity_1.title: Tap Control
steps: Find a water tap in your house.
Open the tap slightly and observe the water flow.
Open the tap fully and observe again.
Observe how a small movement of the tap changes the amount of water flowing.

activity_2.title: Control Something Bigger
steps: Turn ON a fan or light using a switch.
Notice how a small finger movement controls a big device.
Try this with 2 different devices in your house.

extra_exploration.task: Find three things in your house where a small action controls a bigger result.
examples: TV remote button controlling the TV
Doorbell button ringing a loud bell

think_and_notice: What happens when you move the tap a little versus a lot?
How does a small button or switch control a bigger device?
Why do you think machines use small controls instead of large ones?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand control mechanisms
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how small actions can control larger systems.

learning_outcomes.title: Recognize control systems in everyday life
learning_outcomes.description: Students identify real-life examples where small inputs influence bigger outputs.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and reasoning skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze cause-and-effect relationships in daily situations.

learning_outcomes.title: Build curiosity about how machines work
learning_outcomes.description: Students begin connecting everyday controls with technology systems.

bonus_activity: Look around your house and find three devices that are controlled by buttons or small signals.
Examples: TV remote, elevator buttons, washing machine control panel, microwave buttons
Observe how one small button can control a larger machine.

activity_1.title: Observe a Moving Machine
steps: Find a device in your home that rotates or spins.
Turn it ON and carefully observe what part of the machine moves.

activity_2.title: Change the Direction
steps: Take a small toy car or spinning toy.
Push it forward gently.
Push it in the opposite direction.
Observe how the direction of motion changes.

extra_exploration.task: Look around your house and find 5 things that move or rotate using energy.

think_and_notice: Which part of the device was moving or spinning?
What do you think makes that part move?
Can machines work if nothing inside them moves?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your ideas with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand motion in machines
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how machines create movement.

learning_outcomes.title: Identify energy converting into motion
learning_outcomes.description: Students recognize that energy can cause objects to rotate or move.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students carefully analyze how devices around them operate.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect daily experiences with technology
learning_outcomes.description: Students relate household devices to engineering concepts.

bonus_activity: Find three devices in your home that spin or rotate.
Examples: fan, mixer, toy car wheels, washing machine
Observe how these devices use energy to create movement.

activity_1.title: Control Water Flow
steps: Find a water tap in your house.
Turn the tap slightly and observe the water flow.
Open the tap halfway and observe again.
Open the tap fully and observe how the flow changes from slow to fast.

activity_2.title: Control Speed
steps: Find a device where you can adjust the speed or level.
Change the level slowly.
Observe how the speed or sound changes step by step.

extra_exploration.task: Look around your house and find 3 devices that allow gradual control instead of just ON/OFF.

think_and_notice: What happens when the tap is opened a little versus fully?
How does changing the fan regulator affect the speed of the fan?
Why do you think machines sometimes need slow, medium, and fast levels instead of just ON and OFF?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand gradual control
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how systems can change levels smoothly instead of simply turning ON or OFF.

learning_outcomes.title: Identify adjustable systems in daily life
learning_outcomes.description: Students recognize devices that allow control over speed, brightness, or volume.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and analytical skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how changing a control affects a machine’s behavior.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect real-life observations with technology
learning_outcomes.description: Students relate household control systems to engineering design.

bonus_activity: Find three knobs or dials in your home.
Examples: gas stove knob, fan regulator, speaker volume knob
Turn them slowly and observe how the output changes step by step.

activities.topic: Repeating Patterns and Timing in Systems

activity_1.title: Observe a Repeating Pattern
steps: Find something around you that repeats the same action again and again.
Watch the pattern for 30–60 seconds.
Observe how the action repeats over time.

activity_2.title: Create Your Own Rhythm
steps: Clap your hands slowly five times.
Clap faster five times.
Clap in a steady rhythm.
Observe how repeating actions can create patterns or timing.

extra_exploration.task: Look around your house and find three things that work in a repeating cycle.

think_and_notice: What happens when something repeats the same action again and again?
Did the pattern stay regular or change over time?
Why do you think machines follow timed patterns?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Recognize repeating patterns
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe actions that occur in regular cycles.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand timing in systems
learning_outcomes.description: Students identify how machines perform tasks in timed intervals.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and reasoning skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze patterns and predict repeating events.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect real-life patterns with technology
learning_outcomes.description: Students begin relating everyday cycles to how automated systems operate.

bonus_activity: Find two devices in your home that work automatically with timing.
Examples: microwave timer, washing machine program, alarm clock, automatic lights
Observe how these devices perform actions after a certain time interval.

activities.topic: Checking Connections and Troubleshooting in Devices

activity_1.title: Battery Check
steps: Find two devices in your house that use batteries.
Check whether the device is working properly.
Remove the battery and insert it again correctly.
Observe what happens.

activity_2.title: Connection Check
steps: Find a device that uses a plug and wire.
Check if the plug is properly connected.
Check if the wire is bent or loose.
Turn the switch ON and observe if the device works.

extra_exploration.task: Look around your home and find three devices that sometimes stop working.

think_and_notice: What happens when the battery is placed correctly vs incorrectly?
What happens if a plug or wire is not properly connected?
Why do you think engineers check and measure things instead of guessing?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand the importance of checking systems
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe that devices work only when connections and power are correct.

learning_outcomes.title: Identify simple problems in everyday devices
learning_outcomes.description: Students recognize issues such as loose wires or weak batteries.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop troubleshooting skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students learn to check possible causes when something does not work.

learning_outcomes.title: Build an engineering mindset
learning_outcomes.description: Students understand the importance of testing and verification.

bonus_activity: Find three devices in your house that use electricity or batteries.
Before using them, check: power source, switch, and connections.
Observe how small checks can help devices work properly.

activity_1.title: Create a Simple Signal System
steps: Take a bell or buzzer toy (or use a clap sound) and a torch or mobile flashlight.
Turn ON the torch.
At the same time, ring the bell or clap your hands.
Observe how two signals happen together.
Repeat this activity 3–4 times.

activity_2.title: Control a System
steps: Find a device that uses a button or switch to start an action.
Press the button or switch.
Observe what happens when the device starts working.

extra_exploration.task: Look around your house and find three systems where multiple parts work together.

think_and_notice: What happens when you start a device using a button or switch?
Do multiple things happen together (light, sound, motion)?
Why do machines use multiple parts working together?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand systems made of multiple parts
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe that machines consist of components working together.

learning_outcomes.title: Recognize cause-and-effect relationships
learning_outcomes.description: Students understand how one action can trigger multiple outcomes.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop systems thinking
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how different elements interact within a system.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect real-life systems with engineering concepts
learning_outcomes.description: Students relate everyday devices to how circuits and machines are designed.

bonus_activity: Find one system in your home that gives both light and sound signals.
Examples: doorbell camera, mobile phone notification, alarm clock
Observe how different signals work together to communicate information.

activities.topic: Problem Solving and Basic Design Thinking in Electronics

activity_1.title: Observe a Problem
steps: Walk around your house and find one small problem that happens regularly.
Think about how this problem affects daily life.
examples: Lights left ON in empty rooms
Doorbell not heard in another room

activity_2.title: Think of a Simple Solution
steps: Imagine a simple system that could solve the identified problem.
Draw or describe your idea in your notebook.
examples: Alarm when water tank is full

extra_exploration.task: Look at three systems in your house that already solve problems.

think_and_notice: What problem did you observe at home?
What simple system could solve that problem?
How do machines help people in everyday life?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your ideas with your parents or family members.

learning_outcomes.title: Identify real-life problems
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe common issues in their surroundings.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop problem-solving thinking
learning_outcomes.description: Students think of possible solutions using simple systems.

learning_outcomes.title: Apply creativity and innovation
learning_outcomes.description: Students imagine how technology can improve daily life.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect learning with real-world applications
learning_outcomes.description: Students relate electronics concepts to practical uses.

bonus_activity: Look around your home and identify three machines that automatically perform tasks.
Examples: washing machine, automatic water pump, microwave timer
Think about how electronics might help these machines work automatically.
